utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I can and I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, you may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Good morning, Anna Richterova, Julian Nicholls and Denise Gustin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good morning to you. Appearances for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I'm attorney Milan Trbojevic and I have with me Marela Jevtovic, our assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. Good morning to you. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have two matters to raise which concerns our coming witnesses, 7.53 and 7.66.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: The first thing is it possible to go to private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just to make sure that we are all aware of this, that all the sittings of this week will be heard in the morning and not in the afternoon. All right? And the same applies for next week except that on Tuesday, we will not be sitting at all, it being a UN holiday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome back. Please go ahead by repeating your solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. Yes. Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. I hope you had a restful weekend. I'm going to first ask you just a few follow-up questions to clarify some matters I think might not have been perfectly clear on the record from the last time we were speaking together and then I will ask you some questions about leaving the stadium and leaving Bosanski Novi, okay?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: First, when we spoke on Friday about the surrender of weapons by the residents of Suhaca and then the search of the homes in Suhaca, you talked about how the people were gathered in Josava, the residents of Suhaca. Can you just tell me where did people gather? Was that in a building or what kind of place during the surrender of the weapons and the search?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That day, we gathered on a large field at the entrance to the village of Josava and it was not inside a building.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. You also spoke about the shelling of Suhaca and that was on page 13963 of the transcript, and you said something to the effect that most of the shelling was in the area near the mosques and I should have asked you, were the mosques in Suhaca damaged during that shelling?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After the surrender of weapons, three days later the shelling began. The mosques were targeted the worst but they were not badly damaged. It was later on that the mosques were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown P1683.25? It's a photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, I haven't shown you that photograph before. Have you ever seen that photo before, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I haven't seen the photograph before but I know the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you tell me -- you say the mosque. Can you tell me which mosque this was and where it was located -- where it is located?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is the mosque in the Suhaca village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if you can tell us, do you know whether this damage was caused by the shelling or later, as you said that later on the mosques were further destroyed or damaged.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: While we were in Blagaj village, we had loud explosions, seven days later two men went to Suhaca village to bring a man who was killed. He was Numan Dedic. On that occasion, they saw that the explosives had been set to the mosques and the minaret was lying on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I know you weren't there at the time of the explosions but do you know who damaged the mosque, who set these explosions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. That's not something I saw with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. You talked several times on Friday about this man Ranko Balaban, the Josava SDS representative. Can you tell me, if you know, what his profession was before the war or what his job was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what his job was but I know he was a mechanic by profession.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I have one question before we move on to the things we haven't covered, and that is about the relationship between this man and the SDS and the military which you personally observed. Just to recap, you talked on Friday about the negotiations to surrender weapons for Suhaca being conducted by the SDA representative from your village, Barjaktarevic, and Mr. Ranko Balaban. If I understood you correctly, while you were held at the Japra company, prior to being put on the freight train, the same Ranko Balaban was there and identified Sifet Barjaktarevic. And then finally, this same man, Ranko Balaban, was present and acted as a guard at the Mlakve stadium -- Mlakve stadium when you were held there and there were also military guards at that same detention facility. During all these times which I've outlined, did you see any conflict between the SDS and the military or can you describe how relations between them were in the situations which you talked about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: During all these days we spent there, it's true it's one and the same man who had been SDS president in Josava. He was later in Blagaj at the stadium. But all that time he was wearing a military uniform and at that time he was considered to be a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to talk now about how you came to leave the stadium. First of all, do you remember which date it was that you left the stadium, that you finally left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember, the 23rd of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you have any advance notice before that date that you would be leaving?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no advance notice but those people who had family in town, as we found out, could sign for the inmates and that's what some people did, so some people who had family in town got out seven days in advance of others.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you explain to me what you mean by sign for the inmates, for the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of these people who were kept at the stadium had close relatives in the town of Bosanski Novi, and the army in fact, their representatives who were stationed at the hotel or at the fire house, gave permission that the certificates that had to be signed could be signed by the family. And that's what some people had done for them by their family, relatives signed for them, the certificate, and some people, about 80 of them, got out earlier than others.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, could you tell me, and we will talk about what was in the certificate, but when did you have your certificate signed? Did you sign it yourself or have a family member do that for you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I signed this document for myself. One but the last day before I got out from the stadium.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And can you tell us just about the process of how that took place, how the men held in the stadium signed these certificates, the day before Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. they were released?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: One day before liberation, soldiers came from the stadium and two men in civilian clothes, I don't know who they were, they brought desks and lined us up on the turf of the stadium and an announcement was read aloud to the prisoners, and a man later called out names. The man whose name was called out had to run and to -- to the desks and then go back to the line after signing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Were you able to read the documents that you signed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I managed to read it, and it was also read out by the prisoner who was designated to read it aloud to everyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And can you tell us what the -- what that document said? I'm sure you don't remember word for word, but what were you signing? What was the effect of that document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document read, "I so and so give up my movable and immovable property and relinquish it to the Republika Srpska, the municipality of Bosanski Novi."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did the document say anything else about where you were going or what you were going to do next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was nothing written about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you sign just one statement or more than one statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I signed only one statement, and I didn't sign anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what happened after these statements had been signed? These documents?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They called out names and on that occasion, they called out 18 people, but they separated only 15 because three had got out a couple of days earlier. So they took 15 of us and took us away.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And was anybody -- were any other men separated at this point from the group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only those 15 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And was anybody mistreated during this process? Can you tell me about how -- a little bit more about how it was actually organised and whether it was done properly? Or not properly but in a respectful fashion.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One man was mistreated. It was Ibrahim Kantarevic. He was a very sick man. During his stay at the camp, he lacked medication and he didn't know what he was doing any more. He was beaten in order to sign the paper and ultimately his brother signed for him. Apart from that, there were no major incidents and the whole thing was carried through more or less the way they wanted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And then can you tell me how you and the other men came to actually leave the stadium?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next day after the signing, an UNPROFOR vehicle arrived and stopped in front of the stadium. While buses and trucks filed into the stadium. We got on to buses and trucks. At that time there were no soldiers around us. They were standing only outside the stadium and these buses and trucks took us across the bridge to Dvor Na Uni.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you know, were all the men released from the stadium on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That day, all the men were released. There were not enough buses so the first groups who arrived in Dvor waited for a couple of hours for the buses to return, and pick up the men who remained at the stadium, but eventually everybody was transported away.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, while you were being transported out, and while you were on the truck or the bus, can you tell me what you saw? Did you see any property damage as you were being taken out of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That day I left the stadium in an open truck, so I could see everything around me, mainly establishments and houses belonging to Muslims were destroyed. The department store was burned down. That's mainly what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you -- were you able to see any mosques as you were being taken out of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One could see both mosques and both were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you see any -- did you see an Orthodox Church as you were being transported?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One could see an Orthodox Church, but that one was not destroyed. It stood there the way it had before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And once you were taken out and you arrived in Croatia, did you meet with any family members? Were you able to reunite?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We arrived in Karlovac where I found my wife. We talked and she told me that she had gone through via Derventa, Rijeka, Zagreb and ended up in Karlovac where the two of us met.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: How many Muslims from Suhaca remained in Suhaca by the end of 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a single one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like to show the witness now Exhibit 1681, please. This is a cantonal court Bihac, 28 October, 1998 record of exhumation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, I believe I showed you this document earlier. If you could look at page 2 of the original in your language, and I'm sorry that the copy is not perfect, the last paragraph on the bottom of page 2, starts on 13 October, 1998, another mass grave was exhumed at the Blagaj Japra Dubrava location and it continues. If you look at the next page, Witness, and look at the fourth paragraph down in the original B/C/S, I'd like you to read that to yourself and just let me know when you're done. That should be the paragraph identifying the men found in that grave.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it, yes. These were found there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you tell me, you've talked about some of these men in your testimony. Can you read out the names of the men who you knew, the names you recognise in that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I knew Hasan Merzihic, who was a waiter in Suhaca, and the two brothers, Isakovic, Nijaz and Karanfil. As with this elderly woman, I had heard about her. Sulejman Burzic, I didn't know him personally but I know that his son-in-law was a conductor on our local bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. And then just let me try to go through this quickly. Sulejman Burzic, that is the man you saw murdered in the Japra company before boarding the train; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And that is true, as well, of Hasan Merzihic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Hasan Merzihic was killed on the road which I was able to see from the train, and the two Isakovic brothers had remained on the bridge after we had crossed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And those are the two brothers which I think you said you saw -- testified that they were -- had their hands tied with wire and their heads were hanging low?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those were the two brothers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I also have the autopsy records of these four persons which the witness can go through and identify as well. They are attached to the same report. Otherwise, I'm finished, unless you think that would be helpful to the Chamber to have him go through the actual reports on these four men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What do you expect to get from him, if he does precisely that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just further authentication, Your Honour, but these haven't been objected to. I think the authentication was stipulated to by Mr. Ackerman so it may not be necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's up to you. I'm not going to tell you whether it's necessary or not because that's something that you ought to gauge, assess.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Nicholls. Mr. Trbojevic? Now, Mr. Trbojevic, who is appearing for the accused in this case, will be cross-examining you. And your duty is to answer all the questions that he puts to you, as fully and as truthfully as you have done with regard to the questions that the Prosecution put to you. You have no right to distinguish between Defence and Prosecution here. That's of course unless we tell you not to answer any particular question. Mr. Trbojevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I should like to ask you a few questions in order to clarify certain things. On the basis of the statement that you gave to the OTP on the 11th of December, 1998. At the very beginning of your statement, page 2, paragraph 7, you talk about the fact that there had been no police station in Suhaca before the war, but that, however, five to six policemen were on patrol in order to protect the village. In Serb villages they were Serb police and in Muslim villages they were Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. It is true that there were no police station in Suhaca and there was just a reserve police force made up of the residents from the Bosanski Novi town. There was no possibility to have a mixed police in Suhaca because the Serbs did not dare go on patrol -- did not want to go on patrol in Suhaca and the Muslims still didn't dare organise themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, somebody had to organise these patrols?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, like I said, a list with names had been made up in Bosanski Novi and volunteers were being sought for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Wasn't the case that the number of people would rotate in Suhaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only in Suhaca but in Donji Agici -- Donji Agici and in other villages. I think that Gojko Davidovic, for instance, was responsible for Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that in Donji Agici and in these other villages, they were -- there were other people, other volunteers, who had volunteered for that task.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, somebody had to issue them weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Bosanski Novi police station, they had given them weapons, ammunition and when the weapons were handed over in Suhaca, they were asked, they were needed to report what they had. The reservists also had to surrender their weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: So if we are still talking about the spring, 1992 --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: This was all part of the Bosanski Novi police station. It functioned as a part of the Bosanski Novi police station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. This was not a police force that had organised themselves on their own. It was not a local Suhaca police. It had all come from Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I assume that there were important reasons to organise these patrols?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There probably were but I was not aware of them. People walked around normally during the day, they did not harass anyone, they didn't even control anyone. I don't know why they moved around the village at all, why they patrolled the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in late 1991, due to the combat activities in Croatia, didn't a large number of soldiers pass through the village carrying weapons, equipment and ammunition?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct. A number of troops with weapons and equipment passed through Bosanski Novi but they did not control them. They just wanted to make sure that there would be no incidents. Some of our neighbours were telling that they were very well equipped, very well paid. One could see them around the village in those days, carrying weapons, riding the local bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: We heard from various witnesses that the reservists who were on leave with weapons caused a lot of problems wherever they went. Was that the case in your village as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They would mostly be drunk, they opened fire. It was perfectly normal type of behaviour when getting off the buses, they would open fire and shoot in the air.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: These patrols, were they tasked with preventing this type of behaviour?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They had that task among others as well but they didn't dare, they couldn't control soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Since the area in question was close to the border, was there a lot of smuggling from one side of the border to the other?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. There had always been smuggling a lot of smuggling in the area, but as soon as the war started, they assumed control over the bridge between Bosanski Novi and Dvor so that activity decreased significantly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Were there any Croatian reservists coming over?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. People who passed through the Japra valley were mostly local residents from neighbouring villages, and I knew most of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, if there were any Muslim members serving in Croatian units, Muslims who had been mobilised into Croatian units, from the area of Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were probably such cases but I guess they were in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Would they come home on leave? Did they show up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: You said that after the election, Serbs dismissed a large number of Muslims from work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Were you referring to the period of early 1991? Because the elections had taken place in 1990?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not from the very beginning. They kept working for a while, but then they were soon being dismissed for trivial reasons. I know of a case of Adem Barjaktarevic, he had organised a rally in Suhaca as a form of protest against these dismissals. Gojko Davidovic and Ljuban, who was a doctor in Donji Agici, also attended this rally. It was a peaceful normal rally but despite that fact, he was dismissed and I think that that was the reason for his dismissal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: On page 3 of your statement, you discuss the issue of negotiations concerning the surrender of weapons, the negotiations conducted by Sifet Barjaktarevic and Ranko Balaban.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: You told us that the weapons had been surrendered, that the village had been searched, and that there were no longer any problems in this respect.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Weapons were handed in. We spent the whole day on a meadow near Josava while they were searching the village. And when they came back they said everything is all right, you can go on with your normal lives, but three days later things got complicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: On page 3 in paragraph 3, you said that in March, 1992, Serbs established a Crisis Staff in Josava and that in Bosanski Novi and Suhaca, you already had an emergency service which was supposed to be excavated in cases of disaster. Are you saying that there had been an emergency staff that was already in place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had to organise something because we felt abandoned by everyone. We didn't have any rights whatsoever. Whenever we made any requests, they were to no avail so we had to organise ourselves in order to have something done. And that is how this convoy was organised. The objective was to try to reach Croatia with as many casualties -- as -- with as few casualties as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Could you be a little more specific concerning the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know much about them. Sifet attended these negotiations and whenever he came back, he would say, "Well, I wasn't able to do anything. They are not letting us be. We have to try and go over to Croatia." But he himself didn't know what would happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: You said that he would convey to you what they had said, that is that they were not letting you go to Croatia. Can we therefore conclude that one of the requests was to go to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But while we were -- when we were in Blagaj, while we were still in our homes, this was not the subject of these negotiations. So it was raised only later on. Yes, later when we were all in Blagaj, while we were still in our homes we didn't plan to leave anywhere. We even thought that we would return home from Blagaj at one point.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the shelling lasted for about five weeks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: And that soldiers appeared after the shelling.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Soldiers would come and ask what was going on almost every day. They would look for Sifet, and they would talk to him, go back in the evening and then they would start the -- and the shelling would start again until the last day, until the 24th, when they said that they could not protect us, that some troops, some soldiers, were in the area in the vicinity of the Agicka Brda and that we should gather together and go to the municipality building in Bosanski Novi. We got as far as Blagaj but could not proceed. They wouldn't let us go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: What soldiers, what troops, are you referring to? Are you referring to local unit from Bosanski Novi or some other units that were unknown to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day, when we were evicted and taken to Blagaj, those were soldiers, military soldiers -- military police, at least that's what we could judge, on the basis of their uniforms, but I knew most of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: So you knew these people, they were local residents?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: When you stopped at the Blagaj bridge, who stopped you, who were the soldiers who stopped you at the Blagaj bridge?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: And you told us that you had arrived in tractors, vehicles, and you also told us that they had offered you to leave all the vehicles behind, but you refused?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we refused because they told us that we should leave everything and board the trains, and they said that -- but they said that the trains were not leaving to Croatia but to Blagaj, and then we went back but they came again and asked for Sifet in order to talk again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: You told us that this time the talks lasted for about 17 days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the options that were on the table? Who wanted what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that they suggested that we should leave everything and go to Doboj by train, that we couldn't go to Croatia, but Sifet requested that we be allowed to go towards Croatia, towards Dvor Na Uni and Hrvatska Kostajnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: What did this offer mean, to go to Doboj, towards central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. They simply requested that we leave everything, board the trains and continue in the direction of Doboj. What this meant, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: The assumption being that you would be transferred to the territory of the federation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well in all likelihood but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Why would Croatia constitute a better option than the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because most of the people had relatives there, over 70 per cent of them had worked in Croatia, for instance, and they had accommodation in Croatia, they knew where they would go once they reached Croatia. As for Banja Luka and Doboj, the situation was not safe. We didn't know where we would end up. Who knows? Maybe even in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Can we therefore conclude that Karlovac and Zagreb were better options because they -- there was no military activity there as opposed to Doboj and Banja Luka, where fighting was going on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. A peaceful area is always a better option, although at the time we didn't know if there was any fighting going on there or not, whether it had finished or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: You described for us what happened to Burzic, Sulejman. Do you know a person by the name of Zarko Janjetovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know. I think he was some kind of leader from a neighbouring village? Well, I don't know about the man who had killed Burzic. I had only heard about Zarko or Dragan, I'm not sure but at any rate the person worked at the Svodna company. I believe his name was Dragan.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: You told us a name -- about a man by the nickname of Trnka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Milan Balaban.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: You told us that he had killed six persons including a man by the surname of Alic nicknamed as Cama, then Sifet who was a postman and then Kemal who had a nickname Cukar or something like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Cukar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: But you didn't witness the killing itself? You were only told about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see it, though I was standing on the road when it happened. There were a lot of other people with -- with me, and there was a lot of commotion. People were shouting and they said that they had already killed someone. So this was when this incident happened, but I didn't see it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because an eyewitness had seen these three men. One of them being Camil Hasic, but others -- there were some other different names that are also involved, and that's why I wanted to know whether you had heard or seen this incident.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I personally didn't see them. But these two were indeed killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Finally, we have come to the convoy. So you were put on this convoy at one point, and if I'm not mistaken you told us that the train was not under escort?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't see anyone. When we stopped in Prijedor, there were some soldiers around the train but when we left, no, they had stayed behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: What about the doors on the rail cars?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were open while we were travelling from Prijedor to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Did anyone try to escape?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Did anyone try to escape from an open rail car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We could have run, but at that moment, we didn't know what to do, where to go, what shall I do, what would I do if I jump off at Prijedor or Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: What was the situation like in Banja Luka? You said that some soldiers were passing by, that they were shouting slurs at you, verbal abuse?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was after we returned, when only people were going back. Well, this Yoya from Romanija, separated us at Ostruzna, separated women and children from men, took us back and then the train stopped at Banja Luka. At that time the train was closed and locked. The doors were locked and even the windows. We had only holes to look through. We could see a couple of soldiers shouting, "May Alija fuck you. Give us a zolja to shoot you all. It is Alija who made sure you ended up like this," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: So at that point, you were not able to get out of the rail cars?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At that point, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: And they returned you to the stadium?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but first we stopped at Blagaj. Then I saw a policeman in a normal blue uniform and this man even offered us water. Two of us got out, found somewhere two buckets and managed to get water to the first two rail cars on the train, and after that the train moved again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: At that stadium, how did you find cover? Under the stands?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we tried to settle down as best we could but we had only the stands to hide under, because we were not allowed to move to the left or right. We had to stick to the stands.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Were there any superior officers at the stadium whom you could call a commander of that camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at the stadium. There were only guards one of which was always the leader of the guard. There were a couple of people behind the stands, on the stands, at the small gate, at the entrance to the stadium, that was how they were positioned, but who was the leader, I don't know. Their main command was at the fire fighting house or at the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: This brings us to the statements you signed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: We had opportunity to see some of these statements here but we no where saw the sentence to the effect that your property was relinquished to Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It said, "I leave all my movable and immovable property to Republika Srpska, the municipality of Bosanski Novi." It said so loud and clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: We had it sometime ago, I can't show it to you now, we were able to look at it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I don't have it with me either.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I won't dwell on it now. You said you left the stadium, that about 18 people remained behind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: 15. 18 were called out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: You say that you no longer know which of them could be alive and which not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about three of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: What about the others? Are you able to tell us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure about the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Your Honour I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Trbojevic. Is there re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour but could we go into private session for one moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session. Do you have any questions? Judge Janu has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Just a minute ago, you were discussing with Mr. Trbojevic the situation that there was possibility to escape from the railway cars. Is it the truth that at that time you were already deprived of your ID cards, ID papers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's true. At that time, I had no papers at all, because we had been searched. Before that, at the Japra company. From the Japra company compound we were put on the rail cars, and at that point the rail cars were still open.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: And my second question is: You described for us the situation when Zoran brought Sifet Barjaktarevic to the edge of the bridge and you said that he pushed him away and then he was shooting at him. Can you remember or could you observe that all this scene was also observed by Ranko Balaban?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was watching also, because he could see it. He was standing not exactly at the bridge but near enough to see it all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: And what was his reaction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No particular reaction. He remained with that group, talking to people, while Sifet was taken away. He didn't even look back to see what would happen to him. He didn't say anything. He remained with his group while the soldier took Sifet away to the bridge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Thank you, that's all.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I have a small question for you, mainly intended to clear -- make clear one of the answers or one of the statements that you made to the investigator in the course of your interview of the 11th December, 1998. Mr. Trbojevic reminded you, drawing your attention to part of your statement, to when you had stated that we did not have a police station before the war, which is indeed what you said in your statement. Then you went on as follows: "Approximately one month before the war, there were five to six policemen who patrolled each village in order to protect it. In the Serb villages, there were Serb policemen. And in the Muslim Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. villages, there were only Muslims. We had wanted a mixed force but Barjaktarevic was not able to negotiate this." Now my question relates to this last part that I'm going to read now. You continued by saying, "We were told by the Serbs that even though we could get along together, the Serbs had to separate from us because there was a threat from the bigger towns such as Banja Luka." What did you mean by this? What was exactly that the Serbs were telling you? What kind of threat were they referring to and you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know that Serbs were saying that there was a threat from bigger towns. They simply didn't want to have anything to do with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So when the statement here says that you told the interviewer the Serbs had to separate from us because there was a threat from bigger towns such as Banja Luka, did you say those words or didn't you say those words? Because this is what the statement says. Perhaps, Mr. Nicholls, you could show him the -- his statement in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Make sure that the interpretation is getting to him correctly. It's the last sentence of the 7th paragraph from the beginning. The paragraph starts with the words, "In my village, it was Sifet Barjaktarevic of the SDA who went." But I am referring you to the very last sentence of that paragraph. What we have in the English and the statement in the English language is, "We were told by the Serbs that even though we could get along together, the Serbs had to separate from us because there was a threat from the bigger towns such as Banja Luka." Did you or didn't you say those words?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did say this. In fact it was their pretext. They didn't want actually to continue living together with us, which later proved to be the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What kind of threat are you referring to here, are you describing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would always quote some sort of -- cite some sort of threat, saying that it was only under pressure that they had to go to war, and when I say "they," I mean Serbs from the surrounding villages, when they would get a call-up summons, they said they had to respond and go to the army because there was a threat. That's at least what they said to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But when you say "there was a threat from the bigger towns such as Banja Luka," what do you mean? Who was threatening whom? Do you mean to say that the Serbs themselves felt that they were threatened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT82 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were threatened by their own authorities, allegedly. They had to go to war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I don't need that document any further, usher, please. So that brings us to the end of your testimony, and you are free to go back to your country of residence. In fact, you will be assisted by the officers of this Tribunal in any way you require to make this possible. On my part, on my own behalf, and on behalf of Judge Janu and Judge Taya as well as of the Tribunal in general, I should like to thank you for having come over to give evidence in this trial. May we also wish you a safe journey back home. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Nicholls, Mr. Trbojevic, we have two options. We can start straight away with the next witness. The curtains are drawn in any case, and we will break in 15 minutes, or we can break now and start after the break. I would suggest that we start straight away with the witness. We get over with the preliminaries and get moving.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes. I agree. I wanted to suggest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes. Get the next witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do I take it that you are receiving interpretation of what I am saying in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You are about to start to give evidence, giving evidence in this trial, and before you do so, our rules require that you enter a solemn declaration, that in the course of your testimony, you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. It's in other words the equivalent of an oath. The text of the solemn declaration is contained on a piece of paper that the usher, the gentleman who is standing next to you, will be handing to you. Please read that declaration aloud and that will be your undertaking with this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. Before we start with the questions, I need to give you some information which will help you put your mind at rest as per your specific requests made to the Prosecutor. I was informed this morning, or rather we were informed this morning, that you had asked for certain protective measures to be put in place, namely that you will not be referred to by your name and surname and secondly that in the course of your testimony, no one would be able to see your face, what we call facial distortion. I'm pleased to inform you that a decision was taken earlier on today, also because there was no opposition on behalf of the Defence team for Mr. Brdjanin, who is the accused in this case, and in fact you are going to be referred to by a pseudonym, you have been given a number. That would be number BT83?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, BT83.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're going to be referred to as BT83. And as we go along, you should be able to switch on video mode and you will see how others will be seeing you on their monitor, if they are following the proceedings. If you switch on video mode now, the technicians are showing you exactly how you appear on the screen. Now the procedure that will be followed is that Madam Richterova for the Prosecution will be conducting the examination-in-chief, putting a series of questions to you, which you are to answer as fully and truthfully as possible, and she will then be followed by Mr. Trbojevic, who is the co-counsel defending Mr. Brdjanin. Madam Richterova, he is in your hands.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. I will show you a piece of paper on which your name is written. Please read the name to yourself and just confirm whether yes or not it is your name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: This would be Prosecution Exhibit P1630, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that goes under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can we go for a moment into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would like to show the witness P1624, which is Bosanski Novi municipality map.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Would you look at this map and see if it looks reasonably accurate to you, and if yes, point out the village in which you lived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: This map is accurate. The village in which I lived, Gornji Agici is here.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And we can also see Donji Agici. How far was Donji Agici from the village of Gornji Agici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: The distance between the two, Gornji Agici and Donji Agici is about five kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What was the ethnic composition of the village of Gornji Agici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: The ethnic composition of Gornji Agici was such that the majority population was Muslim. The village itself Gornji Agici was 100 per cent Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And Donji Agici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: In Donji Agici, the majority population was Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were there any religious properties in Gornji Agici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: There was one mosque.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And in Donji Agici, was there a mosque?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: In Donji Agici, there was also one mosque.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm done for now with the map but you can leave it next to the witness. Correct me if I'm wrong but before the war in Croatia, the relationship between the Serbs and Muslims were generally good?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: Relations between Serbs and Muslims were good in these places.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did the relationship change after the war in Croatia started?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: From the very beginning of the war in Croatia, relations started to deteriorate and as the war continued, the relations became ever-more tense and strained. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court what were these changes? In which area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: The greatest changes were felt at the point when Serb soldiers went off to Croatia, to war. Some returned and others went to take their place, and those who returned brought their weapons and uniforms with them, and continued walking about in uniform, carrying weapons, in villages they would go like that into shops, in coffee bars, wherever they would go, they had a weapon with them, a rifle or a pistol. They never left them at home. In that atmosphere, people started to fear for their fate and normal relations were no longer possible. They could no longer socialise and trust each other as they did before.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think it is the convenient time to have a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So we'll have a 25-minute break now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Witness, during 1992, was there any time in Gornji Agici or in Bosanski Novi in general where Muslims began to be dismissed from their employment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: I'm aware of the fact that in early 1992, four drivers at the Kozaraprevoz company who were dismissed and one who worked at the Autoprevoz Dvor. These are all the cases that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you ever learn what was the purpose of their dismissals?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: From what I heard, they were dismissed only because they were of Muslim faith or ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were there any checkpoints in Gornji Agici or in the area surrounding the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: To my knowledge, the checkpoints were established in Cele, at the access road to Gornji Agici, and in the direction of Sanski Most. This is where I moved around. And there was another checkpoint which was set up in Donji Agici, behind the Ravska bridge, in the direction of Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Who was in charge in -- on these checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: The checkpoints were manned by -- I guess I can call them our neighbours. That is Serbs who were wearing military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And did you pass personally, did you pass any of these checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: I personally passed through the Cele checkpoint on several occasions, going towards Budimlic Japra and Sanski Most, because of the shop that I had in Gornji Agici. So that was my usual line of communication.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were you required to show any documents?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: Whatever the shift at the checkpoint, everybody knew me, whenever I passed through the checkpoint, because, as I told you, those were all our neighbours. So I had no problems whatsoever. I was never harassed while going through this checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When you said that these people were Serbs wearing military uniforms, did you ever learn from them or from other source which unit they belonged to? Which military unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: As for the military unit they belonged to, I never heard anything about this from anyone. So I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were there any other restrictions of movement, apart of these checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: From what I know, there were no restrictions of movement, or any similar measures.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: During this time period, and I'm talking about the period from the beginning of 1992 until May, 1992, were you personally active in politics?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: During the period you mentioned, I was not active in any political organisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were you a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: Yes. I was a member of the SDA, but I was not involved in any particular activity there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Was it the majority party in your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And who was the President of the SDA in Gornji Agici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: The President of the SDA in Gornji Agici was Hajro Nakic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And tell the Court if you remember who other senior SDA members were in the municipality of Bosanski Novi as a whole.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: From what I heard, the Bosanski Novi SDA chapter president was Muhamed Adamovic, and the vice-president was Dzafer Kapetanovic, Resad Berberovic was the secretary. I'm not aware of any -- of anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I now want to move on to talk about the topics of the surrender of weapons. When did you first hear about the fact that you were supposed to surrender weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: The handover of weapons in our village took place sometime in early May. That is it was at that time that we heard about statements being made regarding the danger of the situation and people said that if anyone had weapons, that those weapons should be collected and handed over to the Serb side, either to the Territorial Defence or to one of the checkpoints located in our vicinity. As for the legally owned weapons, it was said that those should also be handed over.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Tell me, this announcement -- I'm sorry, the fact that you decided to hand over the weapons, was it based on some official announcement or was it a discussion among -- among yourselves?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: From my personal knowledge, there were talks at the very beginning. We discussed the issue amongst ourselves and we agreed that the best solution would be for anyone who possessed weapons illegally, that is without a valid permit, to hand them over before the 11th of May, that is some three or four days before the 11th. Hajro Nakic organised a meeting, whose main topic was the handover of weapons, but, however, the whole thing at the beginning didn't go as smoothly as we thought it would.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When you say it -- at the beginning, it didn't go as smoothly as we thought, what are you referring to? What didn't go smoothly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: Once again, it is my -- just my personal opinion that in those days, people were very much afraid of the soldiers that I already mentioned, soldiers who were constantly on the move, passing through the village and leaving in the direction of Budimlic Japra, Krslje, Bosanski Novi. Where ever they went they had to pass through Gornji Agici. They were armed and people were afraid for themselves and their families, and this is why they hesitated about this -- the handover of illegally owned weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You just said that people were hesitant, they hesitated to hand over illegally owned weapons. Tell us, were there legally or illegally owned weapons in your village and what kind of weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: There were both legally and illegally owned weapons in our village. Most of these were pistols, hunting rifles, that were legally owned, and also automatic rifles that had been illegally obtained.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: To your knowledge --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: In Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: To your knowledge, these automatic rifles, how many of them could be in your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: I was never aware of the exact number of any weapons in the village. I didn't simply know that fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you own any weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: I owned an automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: How did you get in possession of this rifle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: I bought my automatic rifle in Budimlic Japra, from a Serb by the name of Boro Marceta. I knew the man, that is I had known him for five or six years, and we were on very good terms. He owned a small cafe on the road to Sanski Most, at the junction to Budimlic Japra, and since I often used that road, I was often wont to pass by, stop by Boro's. I remember one day when I paid him a visit, I realised how difficult it was, how tense the situation was. The number of soldiers was increasing by the day. They were moving on a daily basis on that road, and he suggested, in a friendly manner, that I bought a rifle or a pistol because I didn't have any weapon at the time. I didn't have the money right away but we agreed that I should come back the next day and bring him the money, and that I could take the rifle with me, which is what I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Witness, are you aware whether there, at any time, any organised military actions or defence by Muslims took place in Gornji Agici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: As far as I know, no military action was ever carried out, nor had it been underway or prepared by the Muslims in Gornji Agici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You mentioned that you discussed with Hajro Nakic and among yourselves the possibility to surrender your weapons. Were these weapons ultimately surrendered by people in Gornji Agici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: That evening, at the meeting which I mentioned, a decision was adopted that all illegally and legally owned weapons should be handed over. However, only some people voluntarily agreed to surrender the weapons, but there were others who simply didn't accept this idea because of the money that it had cost them. However, in most of the cases the weapons were surrendered and handed over at a Serb checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court how the weapons were actually turned over?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: The illegally owned weapons were taken by Hajro and two other individuals whom I didn't know to the Krslje checkpoint, and were handed over to the Serbs there. All legally owned weapons were collected by Mustafa Dzafic and Ibrahim Osmanagic, who were both hunters, which is why they acted as representatives in respect of these legally owned weapons, which they collected and handed over to the Donji Agici Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And were there also some negotiations between you Muslims and your Serb neighbours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: Before we were able to see the soldiers positioned on the hills dominating the village of Agici. For instance in the area of Radosi, there were no negotiations whatsoever. We were simply convinced that -- and we believed that the Serbs would not attack us. However, on the 11th of May, 1992, we noticed soldiers in uniform positioned on the hill in the direction of the Radosi village, and the Gavran village as well. They were carrying boxes with ammunition. They had various types of automatic rifles. We were also able to see two cannons. All this could be plainly seen with the naked eye, without any binoculars, because their positions were very close to the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I will stop you here for a second.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can the witness be shown Exhibit P1683.32? And before he has this photo, the witness could show us on the map where these soldiers were positioned. It's 32. It's a village. So at first, can he --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you show us at the map the position of the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: [indicates] In this area, which is marked as Donji Agici, Krslje, Krupska Rujiska, that is the area between these two villages, this is where the Radosi and Gavran elevation points are located. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can we now show the witness the photo?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you assist the Judges and tell them what we can see on this picture?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: On this photograph, we can clearly see the position in Gornji Agici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And on this photo, are you able to show the position of the soldiers you saw on 11th of May?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: Yes, I am. This area here is also part of the village, and to the right side of the village, in the direction of Radosi and Gavrani is the area where these soldiers were positioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm done with the photo but I would like to still have the map on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So when you noticed the arrival of these soldiers, at this stage, did you start some negotiations with your Serb neighbours or even with some Serb officials?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: First of all, after we had seen these soldiers, we started to panic, of course, because at that moment, we realised that all our hopes and expectations that there would in the end be no shooting or attack on Gornji Agici were in vain. We thought -- well, we were trying to figure out what the best solution would be. Of course, we didn't dare go there, to the position where the soldiers were. We didn't dare ask anyone why this was being done. So in the end, I sent over a child, because Hajro Nakic's house was located at the opposite end of the village, and who was -- he was our representative, and he was aware of the situation, and I sent this child to Hajro Nakic's house to fetch him, to call him, so that he can decide what to do, so that he can maybe go and see these soldiers and see if anything can be done to avoid all this. So he went there and he saw for himself what was going on, and he came back and came to my shop, and I was still working regularly in my shop, and he asked me to close the shop and accompany him to Gornji Agici, to see if we can find anyone there, for instance the President of the SDS, Ljuban Vujasin or anyone else who could have any influence whatsoever on these soldiers or their leader, whoever he was, so that the worst could be prevented.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were you successful?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: Of course -- no, we were not. We did manage to reach Gornji Agici and find Gojko from Gornji Agici [as interpreted], Gojko, the Registrar, whom we asked to take us up there to see Ljuban.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I thought that I heard that you said we managed to reach Donji Agici, and in the transcript, it's Gornji Agici. So can you please repeat where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: From Gornji Agici, we went to Donji Agici. Gornji Agici -- from Gornji Agici, when you go in the direction of Bosanski Novi, you go through Donji Agici. As I said, we came to Ljuban Vujasin's house, and he was president of the SDS party in Donji Agici. Gojko called out to him. He was at home. He worked as a paramedic in Donji Agici. As I said, he was at home at the time, but he wasn't willing to come out of his house. He just talked to us standing at his window, and he told us that Hajro and I could go back, that he wasn't interested in what we were suggesting, and that he had no intention of helping us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What happened that day? What happened on 11 of May, 1992, in your village after you returned from Donji Agici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: At that time, Gojko didn't accept to go with us to Donji Agici either, and the two of us couldn't do anything alone. So our mission was totally unsuccessful and all our hopes were crushed. In the meantime, people would -- people could see those troops on the hills. They were seized by panic. Nobody knew what to do. Sometime around 3.00 p.m., the first shot was fired in the direction of our village. From that moment on, it got only worse. Shooting intensified and people found cover wherever they could. There was no sign that the troops were coming down to the village through the field. The distance, as the crow flies, was about one kilometre, we were comforting ourselves with the hope that they were only trying to intimidate us and we just sat there and waited in our shelters. However, as the night began to fall, people decided after all to take their belongings and leave Donji Agici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I will stop you for a second here. What were they shooting at? And I'm referring to the soldiers you saw nearby the village of Gornji Agici.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: As we could see and hear, they were shooting at our houses. They shot at anyone they could see, at anyone who was moving, and at the houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And was there any return of fire from your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: Nobody dared even think about it, let alone do it. We knew very well that if we did anything, fire a single bullet, for instance, it would be enough of an excuse for them to kill the entire village.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: On 11 of May, did the soldiers enter your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: As I already said, until the evening, the troops did not move towards the village. As the night began to fall, the residents of our village started fleeing towards Donji Agici, but that night, the troops did not enter the village. About half of the residents managed to get across that night to Donji Agici, and the next morning, I put my two children, wife, mother and sister in a car and took them to a hamlet of Dedici, near Donji Agici, and put them up with a relative. That morning, the shelling of the village began.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Witness, were you able, closely observe these soldiers? Were you able to recognise any of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: They were not far away, but still I couldn't recognise any of the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: At any stage, did you learn who they were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: Yes. I found out later, in Prijedor, from the residents of the other half of the village who began fleeing only the second day, after the shelling began, when the troops began to move towards the village. A relative of mine told me then that he recognised two soldiers. They were from Mala Novska Rujiska which is a small village not far from Donji Agici, in the direction of Rudice and Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You stated before I interrupted you that on 12th of May, the shelling started, and also that the soldiers started moving towards the village. What did you do personally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: At that moment, I had no hope whatsoever. I realised there was no hope that this would stop or that it could be prevented. So I decided to flee as well to Donji Agici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You went to Donji Agici. Were there other people from your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: As I said before, in my estimate, about half of my village was already in Donji Agici at the time. As the shelling began, more and more people were coming in on all sorts of vehicles, cars, tractors, on foot. Some of them had been injured and wounded in the meantime. They were all panic-stricken. We were only praying to God that everyone would manage to find their way to Donji Agici and that we would be able to do something to escape the worst. In the meantime, we again asked this Gojko, the Registrar, since Ljuban Vujasin was refusing all our suggestions, we asked this Gojko to go to Gornji Agici and see what became of the people who remained behind and to see what the situation was. He must have realised the condition of the people who were fleeing, and he agreed. We were waiting for him to return from Gornji Agici, to hear news from him, to see if a solution would be found. However, when he came back, he simply said he wasn't able to help us. He said the best thing for us to do was to go on to Bosanski Novi or Prijedor if we possibly could.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You mentioned this person Gojko. Do you remember his surname?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: I think his last name was Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And was he a Serb or a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: He was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You stated that when he returned, he said that it would be best thing for you to leave. Did you leave and where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: Yes, I did. After hearing what Gojko had to say, I decided to move on, never mind where, to Bosanski Novi or Prijedor, as long as we didn't stay there, because his opinion was that if we all gathered in Donji Agici, the village would automatically become a target, and it would be too dangerous to stay there. It would be too dangerous because there were soldiers, troops, on the surrounding hills who might possibly decide to move in and commit a massacre. So we filled about ten cars with people and decided to try and make our way with our families to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you show us at the map the way, the route, which you took to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: We used the road from Donji Agici, Miska Glava, Ljubija, Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Before you decided to go to Prijedor, did you intend to go a different direction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: When we were in Donji Agici, we had already been told that we could not go to Bosanski Novi because the bridge was blocked and there was a checkpoint through which Muslims were not being let through, and that was the road that goes from Hozici via Suhaca, Blagaj to Bosanski Novi. That is why we decided to go the other way, to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And where did you end up in Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: I've already shown you, from Donji Agici we went through Miska Glava and Ljubija and we reached Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And which part of Prijedor did you stay?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: [redacted].

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And do you know where the rest of you stayed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think, Madam Registrar, this needs to be redacted, please. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Where did the rest of you stay in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session for this part, straight away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session. So, Witness, you were then, to your surprise, taken to Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: I stayed in Keraterm until the 18th of June, 2002. On that day, a minivan came in the morning, parked in front of the hall number 2 where I was detained.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I really want only to hear from you very briefly, while you were in Keraterm, were you interrogated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: I was interrogated once in Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were you told why you were in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: During the interrogation, they asked me why I was in Prijedor, why I had been in Prijedor. Of course, I told the truth. I said I had been a refugee who had fled from his own village, Gornji Agici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were you charged with any crime?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: No. They didn't charge me at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And while in Keraterm, were you personally beaten? And answer just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And did you witness that anyone else would be beaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And did you witness that anyone would be killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I do not intend to lead any evidence, any further evidence, on Keraterm, because we have already introduced enough evidence. You stated that on 18 of June, a van arrived and you were taken away from Keraterm. Where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: From Keraterm, I was transported along with another nine men from my village, and we were told that we were going to be taken to Bosanski Novi because we were residents of the Bosanski Novi municipality. So we were taken to Bosanski Novi via Svodna and Blagaj.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And in Bosanski Novi, where were you taken?
