utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: We were taken to the SUP building, the building of the secretariat of the interior in Bosanski Novi. The vehicle stopped outside the building. We were taken out of the vehicle and taken to the basement, to a room without windows. It had a concrete floor and there were two or three small desks with a couple of chairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Bosanski Novi SUP building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: We stayed there for three days. On the third day, we were transferred to the Mlakve stadium where we found other inmates from the Japra valley.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Witness, during these three days in Bosanski Novi SUP, were you interrogated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: I was interrogated once in Bosanski Novi SUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were you asked to write a statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: After the interrogation, I was told to put in writing what I had said, and I complied.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you confess that you owned a weapon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: Yes. I confessed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And by the way, what did you do with this weapon? Did you surrender the weapon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: I had left my weapon at home. I put it on top of the freezer.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Apart from the interrogation, how were you treated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: I wasn't beaten while at the SUP. There were some verbal abuse during the questioning, when they were trying to convince me to admit to certain things I couldn't admit to because I hadn't done them, but there was no beating, just yelling.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: During these three days, how many times did you receive food?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly how many times we were given to eat, but I know we didn't get three meals a day. A couple of times they brought us some food that was not very good quality, to put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And you already stated that you were kept in a room without windows, that there were some chairs and desks. Were there any beds or, if not, where did you sleep?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: There were no beds. Some slept on chairs, some on desks, others on the floor. We tried as best we could to get some sleep.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And you already stated that after these three days, you were transferred to the Mlakve stadium. Can you very briefly tell us about conditions in Mlakve stadium and very briefly, did you have enough food?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: In my view, the conditions at the Mlakve stadium were much better than those at Keraterm or at the Bosanski Novi SUP, meaning that we were not subjected to too much mistreatment or beating, and at that moment, that was the thing that mattered to us the most. The food was extremely bad. As for sleeping arrangements, 700 of us had to find enough room to sleep under the stands, and there was not enough room. Since the food was as bad as it was, some people fainted, and as for washing, you could have a shower with icy water under the stands. In my opinion, until the 22nd of July, 1992, I was able to bear it somehow at the Mlakve stadium.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And what happened on 22nd of July? Were you released from the Mlakve stadium?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: On the 22nd of July, in the morning of that day, a dozen of military policemen arrived at the stadium, carrying some papers in their hands. Up until that moment, the camp was secured by military units, not military policemen. And it was at that time that we were able to see that there would be some sort of change, that there would probably be a roll call, that they would call out names, which is indeed what happened. One of them stood on the side and called out the names of all the detainees, told them to form a single line, and to listen to what he had to say, to what he was going to read. He proceeded by reading out that the next day, on the 23rd of July, a convoy was supposed to leave the territory of the Bosanski Novi municipality, carrying Muslim population, that it had all been organised in advance, and that the majority of the detainees would join this convoy and leave in the direction of Croatia. Then he said that he was going to read out the names of some people and that those people whose names he will read out should go over to the running tarmac and form a single line over there. So he started reading the names from the list, one by one, and he finally read out some 18 names, but out of these 18 people, three had already been released from the stadium. I don't know the circumstances of their release. So he ended up with the number of 15 of inmates, including myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And these 15 people, where were they taken from the Mlakve stadium? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: The 15 of us were told to form a column in pairs, and they tied our hands with handcuffs, and they gave us each an oar. These oars were normally used by the local athletes in Bosanski Novi. At that point, they told us to -- that we were going to the Una Hotel for some additional interrogation. They also said that we would probably have to stay behind this convoy.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I want to show the witness map P1623. It is Bosanski Novi town map.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you show us where were you taken from, what was your route, to Una Hotel, and where the Una Hotel is on this map?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: The Mlakve stadium is located here, in the village of Mlakve, on the outskirts of Bosanski Novi in the direction of Otoka and Krupa. And this is where we left in a column. We passed through the neighbourhood of Vidorija and went along the quay, along the Una River, passed by the secondary school building and reached the Una hotel over there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Only to clarify, this Vidorija it is a suburb of Bosanski Novi town. Who lived in Vidorija? Was it a Serb neighbourhood or was it a Muslim neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: As far as I know, I think that the majority of the population were Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And while we have the map, I will -- we will return to Una Hotel but I only want to ask you where were you taken from Una Hotel? Were you allowed to join the convoy or were you detained at some other place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: Let me first tell you that on the way to the hotel, we were mistreated on several occasions by those military policemen. Some of us were even beaten on the way to the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Witness, I will ask you all details about Una Hotel. I only want you to tell us now where were you taken from Una Hotel? Were you allowed to join the convoy or were you taken to some other place? Just answer me this question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: We were taken to the cellar of the hotel, and placed in a small, dark room.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: From the Hotel Una, how long did you stay? Just tell me how many days you stayed in the Hotel Una?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: We stayed at the Una Hotel for three days.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: And then from the hotel --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You were taken where?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: We were taken to the fire department in Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Because we have this map, can you show us where is Vatrogasni Dom on this map?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: The Bosanski Novi fire department is located here.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And do you still remember whether you walked to Vatrogasni Dom the same way as you were taken to Una Hotel or whether you were taken there in a van?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: We went to the fire department on foot, in two or three columns, not altogether.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now, I will return to the Una Hotel and tell us -- and you already mention it, that you were taken -- you were taken inside of the hotel and where were you taken, in which room were you taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: As I have already indicated, we were placed in the cellar, in a concrete room, which of course had no windows and therefore no light came in. I think it was about 15 square metres large.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were there some other people in this cellar when you -- when you enter it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: Since the cellar was dark, there was no light at all, we couldn't see anyone. However, on the basis of the noise and the voices that were coming from the dark, we realised that there were four men in the room.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You spent three days in this cellar. Where did you sleep? Were there any beds?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: In the cellar, in the room where we were, there was nothing except for the concrete floor and us, those of us who were there, and we spent days and nights there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were you able to use toilets?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: We didn't have a toilet there, nor was it possible for us to call anyone, if any one of us needed to go to the toilet, because we were left alone, and for as long as they didn't need anything, we had no one to address ourselves to. So only if they came to see us, to call us out, to beat us, and to force us to admit all kinds of things that were not true, were we able to see them. Otherwise, we didn't see or hear anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So if you wanted to use a toilet, how did you solve it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: Those who needed the toilet did it in the corner, in a corner of the room.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you receive enough water? Did you receive enough food, during these three days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: When the convoy arrived, the convoy carrying the Muslim population, when it arrived in Karlovac, terrible mistreatment took place.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I will ask you about this but my question was whether you received enough food and enough water. I will -- we will discuss the mistreatment after this.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: Before that time that I just described, we had received only two meals. So we got two meals during a day and a half approximately, and they consisted of some kind of soup or a stew, but when these military policemen burst in and told us that the convoy had arrived in Karlovac, and that the Muslims were declaring over there all kinds of things that were not -- untrue and that they were telling lies and inventing things, such as bad conditions at the stadium, the fact that they were forced to eat grass and so on and so forth, whether this was all true I didn't know. All I know was that it was from that moment on that we were exposed to terrible mistreatment and beatings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sir, I hate to butt in like this but I think I need to. Two things: I would like you to restrict your answers strictly to the question that is put to you from time to time, and not to tell us other things that have got nothing to do with the question as such. That's number 1. Number 2, in my opinion, you still haven't answered the question that was put to you. The question referred to those three days in which you were kept in that cellar in the fire station and the question was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Una Hotel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question was during those three days, did you receive enough food and enough water? Because you answered in a way that I personally don't really believe that you were talking about those three days.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Witness, you heard the Judge. So please just briefly tell us, during these three days, did you receive any food, what kind of food? Did you receive water?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: As I have already said, we received two meals during those -- during that one day and a half, some kind of soup or a stew. We didn't get anything to drink. And then after those two days, after the mistreatment and the beatings started, we got some sandwiches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And water? Nothing absolutely nothing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, nothing to drink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That's clear enough now. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned this mistreatment. First, I want to know who were the people who mistreated you? Did you recognise any of them? Did you know anyone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: Those who mistreated us were military policemen from Bosanski Novi. At that time, they were living in the Una Hotel, and one of those who harassed us was a man whom I knew by sight, and I also know his family name, Kreco. He was the one who on the second day, after the arrival of the convoy, brought a Muslim book, the title of which was "Ilmehal" and let me also add that he was not a military policeman serving with this unit. He was wearing an ordinary military uniform. He tore pages from that book, one by one, and he told us that we had to eat it all. The reason, as he said, was he had simply come across this book in a Muslim house and that by eating this book, we would be able to memorise it better.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Witness, now I want to ask you, and you mentioned that you were mistreated, now you will explain to us this type of humiliation. Were you also beaten during these three days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: As I have already stated, we were terribly beaten after the arrival of the convoy. They used all kinds of objects to beat us up, such as baseball bats, plastic, rubber batons, they hit us with their hands, kicked us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And was it done by this military -- members of this military police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: This was all done by the members of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And we also discussed that after these three days in the Una Hotel, you were taken to Vatrogasni Dom. Were you taken to Vatrogasni Dom by the same military policemen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: We were taken to the fire department by those same military policemen because they were also transferred at the time we were transferred. They no longer stayed there. They were moved to the fire department. And in my estimate, there were over 40 of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know who was -- who was commander of this military police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: The commander of the military police at that time was Bogdan Grab from Josava, whom I had known from before.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Witness, in your statement, you used the name Ratko Grab. So what Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. is the correct name of this person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: The correct name of this person is Bogdan.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So it was just a mistake you made in your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When in Vatrogasni Dom, can you -- can you tell us where were you kept in this Vatrogasni house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: We arrived at the fire department and were immediately thrown into the cellar, which looked like a garage. It consisted of concrete walls with no windows at all. It was somewhat larger than the cellar we were in at the hotel. It must have been between 25 and 30 square metres large.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And how many people were there with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: As I have already mentioned, there were 15 of us from the stadium, plus the four men whom we had found at the hotel. So 19 in total at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And were you kept the whole time in this cellar? Did you also sleep in this cellar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: Yes. We were kept in the cellar the whole time, which means we also slept there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What did you sleep on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: We slept on wooden pallets, which we found outside the fire department, outside the building at the moment we arrived. But then they said that they were there for us and that we should take them down to the cellar and use them to sleep on or sit on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you receive the -- any blankets?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: We didn't get any covers whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Tell the Judges what sort of food you received while in Vatrogasni Dom.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: In the fire department, we would usually get what was left over by the military policemen. That is, we got the same food that they ate. If anything remained, or was left over, we would get it. Sometimes half a day later or the next day, when they were in good mood, sometimes they would bring the food on time but not very often. Usually, they would leave the food to go bad and would bring it down to us with the excuse that the cooks had poured some vinegar into the food so that we would get better appetite. Those were of course very difficult moments for us. We had stomach problems and of course going to the toilet also became problematic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We have to stop here for the time being. We'll have a 25-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Richterova?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Witness, before the break, we discussed the food you received and you also stated that there were some stomach problems and going to the toilet also became problematic. Tell us, were there toilets in the room you were kept?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: There was no toilet in that room.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: If you wanted to use toilet, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: If there was no military policeman outside the room, we had to go to the bathroom inside our room.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And you just said that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand that. If there was no military -- the question was, "If you wanted to use a toilet, where did you go?" And you answered, "If there was no military policeman outside the room, we had to go to the bathroom inside our room." So you used -- you had no toilet in your room, nothing? So you used the corner --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. That's clear now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, to make it absolutely clear, it means that you did whatever you -- was necessary in the corner of your -- of your room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you get maybe some buckets?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: There was nothing there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And if there were a military policeman outside of the room, where were the toilets which you were allowed to use?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: In that case, we could try to ask the policeman for permission to go up to the toilet at the fire department house, where the military policemen were stationed, were quartered. There were two toilet cabins there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And my last question in connection with the usage of the toilets, how long, just tell me how long you stayed in Vatrogasni Dom? Just answer me this question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: I stayed there until the 31st of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So it means you stayed there over one month, and you were using a corner of your room as a temporary toilet. Was this room ever cleaned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: Every day, a group of us would be ordered to clean the corner where we all relieved ourselves, and to remove the excrement from the room.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And now I will ask you about water and be please brief. Did you have enough water to drink?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: We did not have enough water.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you receive any water?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: Occasionally, we would get fresh water, but it was easiest to get drinking water when we went to clean the rooms upstairs at the fire department house, where the military policemen were quartered. There were details assigned every day for this task and it was the easiest way, the best opportunity, to go to the toilet and to find drinking water.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were you allowed, or was it possible for you to wash yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: We had no facilities for washing or showering. Later on, we would be taken sometimes to the Una River, where we could splash ourselves a little. They took us there so that when they beat us, it would hurt more because of the wet clothes we were wearing.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And my last question about this -- in this topic is: Were you able to change your clothes while you were either in Vatrogasni Dom or in Mlakve stadium?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: In the time we spent at the Vatrogasni Dom, we had no opportunity at all to change because we were not allowed any visits, nor did they give us any change of clothes. At the Mlakve stadium, some visits were allowed, depending on who was on guard, depending on the disposition of soldiers who were on shift at the time. They would call out the names of inmates whose family came to visit them, and on those occasions, some people received a change of clothes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Witness, before I move on to talk about your treatment in Vatrogasni Dom, I want to hear from you very briefly your daily routines in Vatrogasni Dom, but please very briefly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: From day 1, at the Vatrogasni Dom, from the moment we arrived, they showed us the room where we would be kept and the pallets on which we were to sleep. We had to carry the pallets inside. We were taken to the embankment. They called out six of us and took us to the quay near the Vatrogasni Dom, in the direction of the Una River, of Dvor Na Uni. Some 50 metres behind the fire department house, we set concrete urns that had been previously used for decorations and for flowers. They were supposed to serve as a barrier blocking the passage of vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Witness, to make it more easier, I will ask you: During the whole stay in Vatrogasni Dom, were you forced to work or, if I rephrase it, did you have to perform work obligation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: Well, the tasks I described were the beginning of our work obligation at the Vatrogasni Dom. I also mentioned that every day we had to clean the premises of the fire department house and I must say the conditions there were incredible because at all times, out of those 40 military policemen, five to ten were drunk and they created a terrible mess, breaking things, and creating a mess that we were supposed to clean up. We had to clean also the area around. Every day they would take us to the wall, to the Una River.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: We don't need to go into these details. You answered my question that you had to perform this work obligation. Now I want to ask you, during your stay in Vatrogasni Dom, were you generally -- were you beaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: Yes, they did. They did beat us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Who did -- who beat you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: All the time that we spent at Vatrogasni Dom, we were beaten. The main perpetrators of these beatings were military policemen from the fire department house, and in addition to them, there were soldiers who would occasionally be brought in, who had come from various front lines, and who would go about town creating unrest and such soldiers would be brought to our quarters drunken to beat us and mistreat us during the night until the next day.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Witness, did you recognise or -- did you recognise any of these soldiers of -- or military policemen who beat you? And can you name some of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: During the first days, as I said, I recognised the commander of the military police, Bogdan Grab, as well as his brother, who was a regular military policeman. I also knew a man named Mihaljica from Krslje who used to be a neighbour of mine. I also recognised a couple of military policemen whose names I knew, and who were particularly heavy-handed towards the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you give us just a couple of names of people who maltreated you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: Dragan Djuric, Zeljko Bosancic, Miljenko Janjatovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would go back to the beatings. You said that these military policemen beat you and some other soldiers. Can you briefly describe how -- how they beat you? What kind of tools they used when they beat you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: I can say straight away that they were not particularly choosey when it came to things to beat us with. They used whatever was at hand. In the beginning, it was mainly baseball bats, plastic or rubber truncheons, and very often, if they had nothing else, they would take a wooden stick and beat us with it. It made them very happy and proud when they could simply beat us all over, using their bare hands or feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I presume that your answer will be yes, but were you personally beaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: Yes, I was beaten.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And can you tell the Judges whether you sustained any injuries?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: Many times I was injured on my head, on my ribs, hands, wrists, shoulders, back.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: While -- what kind of injuries? You just said that many times I was injured on my head, my ribs. Can you just briefly describe what kind of injuries you are talking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: These injuries were around my eyes, in the back of my head, on my shoulders, injuries to my ribs, which were not visible but I knew what they meant.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: During the time in Vatrogasni Dom, was anyone killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you see any -- any killing personally? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you assist the Judges and tell them what you saw?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: The event that I witnessed specifically was the killing of Ismet Muslimovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: How was he killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: That day, when he was killed, was one of the worst days I had spent at the Vatrogasni Dom camp. From the early morning, they started taking people out of our quarters and taking them away behind the Vatrogasni Dom to beat them black and blue. The pretext they used was a defeat they suffered on the front line in Krajina somewhere. He -- they kept beating people up the whole day, and sometime around 5.00 in the afternoon, they took out Ismet and brought him outside the room. He could barely walk, and a policeman had to help him come outside. After the first question, which was why he had been in Prijedor at all, he opened his mouth to answer, when Dragan Djuric hit him with his open palm in his -- on his already-injured head. Ismet fainted immediately. Djuric ordered two inmates to run somewhere and bring a pot of water and splash it on him so that he would come around. They brought the water and splashed it -- splashed it on him but it didn't help. He began to regain consciousness but he couldn't get up. Then Djuric ordered other inmates to take a bucket that was standing next to the door, in which we washed the plates we had lunch from, so the water in that bucket was dirty and greasy, and that water again was splashed on Ismet. Five or six minutes later, Ismet tried to get on his feet and managed. Then this same Dragan Djuric said, "Do you know perhaps where the house of a neighbour of mine from Vidorija is?" We could barely hear Ismet's voice when he tried to answer. He was at the end of his tether. He said that he knew but he couldn't go and show them. Djuric said that two military policemen would come along with him and that he should go with them and show them the place where this man lived. Two military policemen flanked Ismet, picked him up, slightly, and they walked away from the Vatrogasni Dom until they reached a distance at which we were no longer able to see them. [redacted]

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: We are trying to do our best to protect you, not to reveal your identity, and then you mention your own name. So be careful. Okay? In any case, don't worry about it because we are striking it off.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So we finished the two men were called out to help with this man Muslimovic. What did you see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: We got out, me and this friend of mine, and we saw Ismet lying on this wheelbarrow. In the meantime, Dragan Djuric, who was a van driver with the military police, came with the van and he backed to the area behind the fire department, just outside the room where we were located, and he told us to put Ismet into the van.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: At this moment, you saw Ismet Muslimovic, were you able to see what kind, if any, injuries Ismet sustained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: I was about to tell you that. As we were trying to put him into the van, and Ismet was about 1.90 metres tall and at the time he was arrested he weighed about 110 kilos, but got down to 90, 95, in the meantime, we were not able to do it on our own and then Djuric ordered for another man to join us. They fetched a man by the name of Ante, who was from Prijedor by origin, and then the three of us took Ismet out of the wheelbarrow and put him into the van. As we were trying to put him into the van, we realised that his entire body had been fractured and broken and it was easy to see that he was already dead. All his teeth were gone, his neck was dislocated, the elbows were totally limp and it was in this state that we threw him into the kombi, into the van. One of these two military policemen, told one of us to get into the van and come with them. Ibrahimagic got into the van and since Dragan Djuric knew him, they used to work together at the Kozaraprevoz transport company before the war, they were both truck drivers, he said that Ibrahimagic should get out and that Ante should go instead. Which is what happened. Ante got into the van which drove away and Ante never came back.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You just said that Ante never came back. Were there other occasions when people were taken away and never returned? And just answer me yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: Yes. There were many such occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you name at least few people you remember were taken away and never seen again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you give us the name? The names?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: Salko Vukovic [as interpreted], for instance, who was a teacher, worked as a teacher in Donji Agici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, did you say Salko Vukovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: Mukovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you for the correction. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: Razim Veletanlic, also a teacher in Donji Agici. Resad Kapetanovic, whom I already mentioned. He was a vice-president of the Bosanski Novi SDA chapter.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In your statement, you used the name Dzafer Kapetanovic and now you say Resad Kapetanovic. So what is the correct name of this person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: My apologies. The correct name of the person is Dzafer Kapetanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And so I interrupted you. So what was the other person you saw?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: Resad Berberovic, the secretary of the Bosanski Novi SDA branch. Abdulah Huzeirovic from Blagaj. Hasan Isakovic from Suhaca. Fadil Blagajcevic from Blagaj.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: These people you just listed, were they beaten before they were taken away?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you see in which condition they were before they were taken away?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: Those who were taken away and who never returned were in such a bad condition that, in my opinion, they could not survive for longer than a day or two. So they didn't have to be killed. They were just -- they would have died -- they would have died any way. They were left to die.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You mentioned in your statement that on one occasion, a person returned after being taken away. Can you please explain this occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: Obviously those who were taken away were taken away by night. That night, when this happened, they first took away two men at around 10.00 p.m., neither of whom returned. This is just an approximation as to the time because we didn't have our watches on, but it was summertime so it was relatively easy to orient ourselves. That night, eight of us remained in the room.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Witness, I have to interrupt you because we are running out of time and so I would really like to hear only who returned and what did you hear from this person after he returned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: That night, sometime before morning, they took away Hajro and Hasan Isakovic. Hajro is the son of Hasan. An hour and a half later, approximately, Hajro Isakovic was taken back. He returned, which was the first such case since they started taking people away. As he entered the room, he had -- he was blindfolded and one of the military policemen just threw him, pushed him into the room. We whispered asking what had happened, and how it came about that he returned. He was still in a lot of fear, and he managed to tell us that his father had been murdered near the river. Apparently they were asking some money from him, and he said he didn't have any. Hajro was blindfolded and he heard a shot at that moment, which was soon followed by the sound of a body falling into the water. As for Hajro, he was taken back to the fire department in this van. My assumption is that they wanted -- they tried to obtain some information from him regarding this money, because two sons of Hasan Isakovic had already been killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know the names of these two brothers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: Nijaz Isakovic, he was the oldest son of Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: If I can remind you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: I'm really sorry that the name of the other escapes me at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: If I may use the witness statement, is the name of the other brother Karanfil?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And it brings us towards the end. You already stated that after this ordeal, were you released on the 30th of August, 1992. After you were released, and now, really briefly, where did you go? Did you leave the municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: After I was released, I asked if it was possible for me to go back to Prijedor and stay there with my relatives, with whom I had stayed before I was taken to the Keraterm camp, and they said that if I didn't have anyone in Bosanski Novi, any relative living there, or if I didn't know where to go, that I could for the time being, that is that if I didn't have a place to live for a while, that I could go to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And is it correct that after sometime in Prijedor, you finally left for Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And before you -- before you left, did you have to sign any papers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: No. I didn't have to sign any documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, your parents or your family, who left before, did they have to sign any papers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: Later, when we were reunited, I learned that they had to meet the requests of the Serb authorities, that is that they had to pay some kind of bills and settle all their accounts, and leave their property behind.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And my very last question is: Did you at any time learn the fate of the mosques in your village, Gornji Agici, and in the village of Donji Agici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I learned that the mosques had been destroyed, the mosques in Gornji and Donji Agici, as was the case with all the mosques in the Japra river valley.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And did you also learn when was it -- and I mean whether it was in 1992 or at some later stage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT83
utterances.text: According to my knowledge, and from what I heard from others, this happened in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I do not have further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Richterova. That brings us to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the end for today. We will continue tomorrow morning, sir, and when Mr. Trbojevic is expected to start with his cross-examination. So that we can plan a little bit ahead, Mr. Trbojevic, how long do you expect your cross to last, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For about 45 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So then you will have the other witness 7.66 in line?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, he will be ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And you should anticipate how long that's going to take. Whether it will probably be the whole morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Most probably the whole session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. After that, we will have 7.73?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, all the witnesses who are scheduled on this list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Do you anticipate -- what's 7.263? I don't have that witness in the Bosanski Novi list particularly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No. She is not from Bosanski Novi. She is a witness from the Prijedor municipality and she testified in the Stakic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. That makes it clear. Okay. Thanks. See you tomorrow morning. Thank you. Make sure that the curtains are drawn before the witness leaves the courtroom.
